report:
## Research Summary: Does Opening a Window/Door Improve Sleep Quality?

**The evidence is mixed but leans toward a mechanistic, not universal, benefit.**

The core mechanism is CO2 buildup. Multiple studies confirm that closed bedrooms accumulate CO2 overnight, and higher concentrations correlate with worse sleep architecture. A DTU study found that when ventilation was reduced and CO2 rose from 856 ppm to 1,927 ppm, participants experienced "shorter deep sleep, longer light sleep, and more awakenings" (https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/bedroom-ventilation-and-sleep-quality-2/). Related DTU research concluded ventilation keeping CO2 below roughly 750–1,000 ppm allows air quality good enough not to impair sleep (https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day). A pilot experiment comparing open-window (CO2 ~660 ppm) versus closed (CO2 ~2,585 ppm) conditions found sleep quality and perceived air freshness improved significantly with better ventilation (ResearchGate, "The effects of bedroom air quality on sleep and next-day performance").

However, opening a window is only one way to lower CO2, and it introduces confounders. A Shanghai study found that while open windows improved air quality, sleep still suffered in summer due to heat and noise (https://www.sleepfoundation.org/sleep-news/open-window-may-be-better-for-sleep-but-we-keep-it-closed). Similarly, outdoor air pollution can worsen respiratory conditions like asthma, potentially offsetting benefits for sensitive individuals (https://aafa.org/asthma/asthma-triggers-causes/air-pollution-smog-asthma/).

**Conclusion:** The claim is generally supported—better ventilation (via open window/door) that reduces CO2 buildup tends to improve sleep quality—but this depends on ambient conditions. If opening a window introduces excessive noise, heat, cold, or polluted air, the benefit can be negated or reversed. The claim is best framed as "ventilation improves sleep when it doesn't introduce worse tradeoffs," rather than an unconditional rule.
